Ultrasonic thickness monitoring at CMLs: technique, calibration and data quality

Short answer: Ultrasonic thickness monitoring means taking repeat UT wall-thickness readings at the same condition monitoring locations (CMLs) over time, so the change between surveys gives a corrosion rate and a remaining life. The readings are only as good as their repeatability: the same location, a suitable transducer, calibration on a reference block near the component temperature, the right technique for coatings, and records good enough that the next survey can match them.

The guide above explains how UT thickness gauging works. This section is about why thickness monitoring programs produce corrosion rates that nobody trusts, and how to fix that. It covers how CMLs are used under API 570 and API 510, transducer and technique choice, calibration, coatings and temperature, spot readings versus scanning, permanent monitoring sensors, and the data checks an inspector should run before using a new survey to calculate rates. For the code-text requirements of ASME Section V Article 5 see our ASME V Article 5 guide.

Why thickness monitoring matters: the arithmetic behind the readings

In-service inspection codes turn thickness readings into decisions. API 570 for piping and API 510 for pressure vessels calculate remaining life as the difference between the actual thickness and the required thickness, divided by the corrosion rate, and the corrosion rate itself is the loss of thickness between two readings divided by the time between them. API 570 uses both a long-term rate, from the earliest reliable reading, and a short-term rate, from the two most recent, and the inspector selects the rate that best reflects current conditions. The inspection interval then follows from the remaining life and the code's limits. API 570 is currently in its 5th edition, published in February 2024; check the current edition of each code for the exact rules and limits.

The consequence is that every reading error feeds into a rate, every rate feeds into a remaining life, and every remaining life feeds into a date. Measurement error divides by the time between surveys. A small reading difference over many years barely moves the rate; the same difference over a short interval can make a stable line look like it is corroding quickly, or make a corroding line look stable. That is why repeatability matters more than instrument resolution in a monitoring program.

The current API 570 term is condition monitoring location (CML), which replaced the older thickness measurement location (TML) to include locations monitored by methods other than UT. A CML is a designated area, not a single point, and the program defines where it is, how many readings are taken in it, and how they are recorded.

Transducer and technique choice

Most corrosion monitoring uses 0-degree longitudinal-wave pulse-echo contact UT. API's defined procedure for its thickness measurement examination program, API-UT-21, describes single-element, dual-element and delay-line transducers in the 1 to 10 MHz range, and it is a useful public reference for good practice even though it was written for the API QUTE-TM performance demonstration rather than for a plant program. ASTM E797, Standard Practice for Measuring Thickness by Manual Ultrasonic Pulse-Echo Contact Method, is the general practice referenced for contact thickness measurement; its scope covers measurement at temperatures not exceeding 200 °F (93 °C).

TechniqueBest useWatch for
Dual-element transducer, first backwall echoCorroded, pitted or rough backwalls; the workhorse for corrosion surveysV-path error at small thicknesses; must calibrate across the expected range
Single-element or delay-line, echo-to-echoPrecise readings on smoother material; measuring through coatingsNeeds a clean second backwall echo; may not work on heavily pitted backwalls
A-scan display gaugeLets the examiner see what is being measured; verifies the echo is the backwallRequires examiner skill to interpret; slower than a digital-only gauge
UT scanning and corrosion mappingFinding the minimum in an area of localised corrosion or pittingMore time per CML; data volume needs management
High-temperature probes and couplantReadings on hot lines without shutdownVelocity changes with temperature; contact time limits; separate calibration approach

Dual-element probes are preferred for corrosion because they handle rough and pitted backwalls, but their angled sound path introduces a known error that grows as thickness decreases. Instruments correct for it, but only if the gauge is calibrated on a reference block that covers the thickness range being measured. A gauge zeroed on a single thick step and then used on thin, corroded pipe will read with a systematic error, and that error does not show up until someone compares surveys taken with different gauges.

A display that shows the A-scan is a quality control tool. It lets the examiner confirm that the reading is the backwall and not a lamination, an inclusion, a doubling echo on thin material, or a coating interface. Digital-only gauges are faster, but where readings matter for remaining life, the ability to see the signal is worth the extra time.

Calibration, temperature and couplant

Calibration ties the instrument's time measurement to thickness. Good practice is a two-point calibration on a step wedge of the same or acoustically similar material covering the expected thickness range, verified at intervals during the work and whenever anything in the system changes. API-UT-21 requires recalibration after any change of search unit, shoe, couplant or instrument, and requires the calibration block to be within 25 °F of the component temperature. Those are the requirements of API's examination procedure; your own procedure, approved by a Level III, may set equivalent or stricter rules.

Temperature matters because sound velocity in steel changes with temperature. A gauge calibrated on a cold block and used on a hot line will misreport thickness by an amount that depends on the temperature difference, and that error recurs every time the survey is done at a different process temperature. For hot surveys, the procedure should either calibrate on a block at component temperature or apply a documented temperature correction, and the component temperature should be recorded with each reading so later surveys can be compared fairly.

Couplant selection affects readings on rough or hot surfaces. API-UT-21 recommends higher-viscosity couplant on rough surfaces. High-temperature work needs couplant rated for the temperature and short contact times to protect the probe. Recording the couplant used is a small detail that helps explain differences between surveys.

Coated surfaces and surface preparation

Paint and coating are the most common hidden source of error. A conventional single-echo reading through coating measures coating plus steel, and because sound travels more slowly in most coatings than in steel, the coating thickness is overstated when converted at steel velocity. A survey through paint followed by a survey on blasted steel will then show apparent metal loss that never happened.

Two approaches avoid this. Echo-to-echo or multiple-backwall measurement times the interval between successive backwall echoes, which excludes the coating; API-UT-21 allows this, or calibration on a coated reference block. Alternatively, coating is removed at the CML, which gives the best readings but must be repaired afterward. Whichever approach is chosen, the record should state it, because mixing approaches between surveys corrupts the rate.

Surface preparation should remove loose scale and corrosion product that block coupling, without grinding into the base metal and creating artificial loss. On insulated equipment, readings are often taken through inspection ports, and the port location becomes part of the CML definition.

Designing CMLs that can be repeated

A monitoring program depends on readings being taken at the same place every time. The owner's inspector selects CMLs based on the damage mechanisms expected for the circuit, including injection points, deadlegs, soil-to-air interfaces, mixing points and areas of turbulence. Practical repeatability depends on how the CML is defined:

  • Physical marking or precise description. Paint marks, stencilled IDs, or a description tied to a weld or fitting. On piping, a reading at a CML commonly includes several points around the circumference, and on elbows the outside radius is often included.
  • Readings per CML. The program should state whether the recorded value is the minimum of several readings, an average, or each reading separately. Changing the rule changes the rate.
  • Isometric drawings. CML locations on current isometrics with unique IDs, so a new crew can find them.
  • Scanning versus spot readings. Spot readings suit uniform corrosion. Localised damage needs scanning of the CML area so the minimum is captured.

Our article on building a CML register that survives ten years covers the long-term data management side, and pipe wall thickness UT procedures covers CMLs, rates and remaining life for piping.

Data quality checks before rates are calculated

Before a new survey is used to update corrosion rates, the inspector should screen it. The common red flags are:

  • Apparent growth. A reading thicker than the previous one by more than measurement tolerance indicates a location, technique or calibration difference, not metal growth.
  • Sudden rate change. A short-term rate much higher than the long-term rate deserves a re-measurement before it drives an interval change, and also deserves a check for a process change.
  • Readings below nominal manufacturing tolerance on the first survey. These may reflect original mill tolerance rather than corrosion; baseline records matter.
  • Missing context. Instrument, probe, technique, coating status and temperature missing from the record make it impossible to resolve discrepancies later.
  • Single readings driving decisions. Where a minimum reading governs remaining life, a confirmation reading or scan at that location is cheap insurance.

Re-measurement at a flagged location is usually quicker than arguing about the rate. Programs that build these checks into the report review step catch most problems before they reach the interval calculation. Ask us to re-measure flagged CMLs.

Permanent ultrasonic thickness monitoring sensors

Some searches for ultrasonic thickness monitoring are about permanently installed sensors rather than manual surveys. These are UT transducers fixed to the pipe or vessel, often wireless or hardwired to a data system, that take readings at set intervals without anyone going to the location. They are used where access is costly or hazardous, such as high-temperature lines, elevated or insulated piping, and subsea or offshore equipment, and where the operator wants trend data at a higher frequency than periodic surveys provide, for example during a change of crude slate or chemical treatment.

Permanent sensors give excellent repeatability because the transducer never moves, so very small changes in wall thickness can be trended. Their limitation is coverage: each sensor monitors a small spot, so it complements rather than replaces surveys and scanning of the wider area. Subsea wall thickness monitoring uses similar principles, with sensors installed on subsea pipework or clamp-on systems deployed by divers or ROVs; those are specialist offshore applications governed by the operator's subsea integrity program.

Where permanent sensors are used for code-required readings, the owner's inspector should confirm how the data is validated and how the sensor locations are recorded as CMLs.

Who should take the readings

Thickness readings feed code decisions, so the people taking them should be qualified for the work. API-UT-21 recommends that thickness examiners be UT Level II, Level II in UT thickness measurement, or UT Level III under the employer's SNT-TC-1A written practice. Some operators also require examiners to pass API's QUTE-TM performance demonstration; that is an API Individual Certification Program credential, and information on it is published on the API ICP website. Atlantis does not provide QUTE-TM training. For the ASNT route, see NDT Level II training.

Common mistakes in UT thickness monitoring

  • Calibrating on one thickness. Dual-element V-path error makes thin readings wrong; calibrate across the range.
  • Measuring through paint with a single-echo technique, then comparing with readings on bare steel.
  • Ignoring temperature. Calibration block far from component temperature without correction.
  • Moving the CML. Readings taken a short distance from the previous spot on a corroded surface are not comparable.
  • Spot readings for localised corrosion. The minimum is missed and remaining life is overstated.
  • Thin records. No instrument, probe, technique, temperature or examiner certification on the report.

Regulatory overlay and Canada

In the USA, thickness monitoring under API 510 and API 570 is the backbone of mechanical integrity programs required under OSHA process safety management, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), where those codes are applied as recognised and generally accepted good engineering practice, and state boiler and pressure vessel laws may reference the NBIC or API codes for in-service inspection. In Canada, provincial regulators set the requirements: in Alberta, ABSA's integrity management requirements govern owner programs for pressure equipment, and other provinces have their own regulators such as TSSA in Ontario. Confirm requirements with your jurisdiction.

More questions about ultrasonic thickness monitoring

What is ultrasonic thickness monitoring?

It is the repeated measurement of wall thickness at the same locations over time using ultrasonic testing, so that the change gives a corrosion rate and remaining life. Readings may be taken manually during surveys or by permanently installed sensors.

What is a thickness monitoring location?

The older term, thickness measurement location (TML), has been replaced in API 570 by condition monitoring location (CML): a designated area where periodic examinations are made to monitor the condition of the equipment, defined so readings can be repeated.

Which transducer is best for corrosion thickness readings?

Dual-element transducers are usually preferred for corroded and pitted backwalls. Single-element or delay-line probes with echo-to-echo measurement suit smoother surfaces and coated components. Calibrate across the expected thickness range.

Can you measure thickness through paint?

Yes, using echo-to-echo or multiple-backwall techniques that exclude the coating, or by calibrating on a coated reference block. A single-echo reading through paint includes the coating and overstates steel thickness.

How does temperature affect UT thickness readings?

Sound velocity changes with temperature, so readings on hot or cold components need calibration near component temperature or a documented correction. API-UT-21 requires the calibration block to be within 25 °F of the component.

Why do corrosion rates from UT surveys sometimes look wrong?

Usually because of location, technique, calibration or coating differences between surveys. Over a short interval, a small reading difference can produce a large apparent rate. Screen new data and re-measure suspect locations before updating rates.

What is subsea wall thickness monitoring?

It is the measurement of pipe or vessel wall thickness on subsea equipment, often by permanently installed or ROV-deployed ultrasonic sensors, to trend internal corrosion where access is very costly. It is a specialist offshore application within the operator's subsea integrity program.

Who can take UT thickness readings for API 570?

Readings should be taken by qualified examiners; API-UT-21 recommends UT Level II, Level II in UT thickness measurement, or UT Level III under the employer's SNT-TC-1A written practice. Some owners also require API QUTE-TM. The authorized inspector evaluates the data.

Have a circuit with corrosion rates nobody trusts? Send us the CML list and last two surveys and we will scope re-measurement. Related: API 570 piping inspection requirements.

Sources: API-UT-21 Defined Procedure for Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement (api.org); API Individual Certification Programs; ASTM E797/E797M-21; ASME BPVC Section V. Confirm requirements against current editions of API 510 and API 570.
